content.text: Context doesn't hold or manage state. It hands one value to every component below a provider, and when that value changes, every component reading it re-renders, whatever part of it they use. Narrow updates by splitting the value along how it changes, and reach for a store with selectors when components need different slices of busy data.

An online shop's category page shows 48 products, each with its own "Add to cart" button. Every click makes the page hitch for a moment. The React Profiler shows why: after each click, all 48 buttons render again, though none of them displays anything about the cart. The only component that needed to change was the item count in the header. Every button calls
, and that same context also carries the items.
The belief: context is React's built-in state manager. Put shared state in a provider, read it anywhere with
, and React re-renders only the components that read the part of the value that changed, the way a store with selectors would.

It's easy to believe because context does replace a lot of what people used stores for. It ends prop drilling, React's docs show reducer and context together as a way to manage state that distant components need, and a small app with a theme and a signed-in user never notices a cost. Reading
even looks like a subscription to one field. It isn't.
Context delivers a value; it doesn't manage it
lets a component make a value available to any component below it, however deep. That's the whole feature. The state behind the value still lives in

inside the provider component, and updating it is ordinary React state: the provider re-renders and passes down a new value. Context adds no update API, no selectors and no middleware. In React's own pattern, the reducer manages the state and context delivers it.
Every reader gets the whole value
React's docs describe the rule: when a provider receives a value that's different under
, React re-renders every component that reads that context, starting from the provider, and
doesn't stop it. React doesn't track which fields a component uses. Destructuring
happens after the read, so a button that only needs
is subscribed to the items too.
An earlier article showed an inline object creating a new context value on every render.
docs recommend it. But memoization can't help when the data inside really changed: a memoized
is still a new object every time an item is added, so every reader renders.
Split the value along how it changes
A context can't select, so you narrow updates by giving each kind of value its own context. React's reducer-and-context guide already uses two: one for the state and one for

The same idea scales to other splits. Values that change on every keystroke shouldn't share a context with the theme or the signed-in user, which change rarely and are read almost everywhere.

When you need a real store

Splitting has a limit. When many components each need a different slice of large, frequently changing data, you'd end up with a context per field. That's the job of a store that lives outside React, where each component subscribes to the slice it selects. React's hook for subscribing to one is
: when the store changes, it re-renders the component only if the snapshot it returns differs under
hooks built on the same idea. React Redux's docs say
after each action and re-renders only when it changed, so a selector that builds a new object every time re-renders every time.

How to apply it in your project
Record a single interaction in the React DevTools Profiler. Look for context readers that rendered but show nothing that changed.
For each context, write down what's in its value, how often each part changes, and which components read which part.

items.title: Move busy, sliced data to a store

content.text: When splits multiply and many components each read a small part of frequently changing data, use a store with selectors.
